sections.title: Validators — Scenario-Based Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
**S1. You're building a job posting system. Implement complete validation with cross-field rules.**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> from pydantic import BaseModel, field_validator, model_validator, Field
> from typing import List, Optional, Literal
> from datetime import date, datetime
> from decimal import Decimal
>
> class JobPosting(BaseModel):
>     title:           str = Field(..., min_length=5, max_length=200)
>     company_name:    str = Field(..., min_length=2, max_length=100)
>     description:     str = Field(..., min_length=100)
>     required_skills: List[str]
>     employment_type: Literal["full_time","part_time","contract","internship"]
>     location:        str
>     remote_policy:   Literal["remote","hybrid","onsite"]
>
>     salary_min:    Optional[Decimal] = Field(None, ge=0, decimal_places=2)
>     salary_max:    Optional[Decimal] = Field(None, ge=0, decimal_places=2)
>     currency:      str = "USD"
>
>     experience_min_years: int = Field(0, ge=0, le=50)
>     experience_max_years: Optional[int] = Field(None, ge=0, le=50)
>
>     application_deadline: Optional[date] = None
>     start_date:           Optional[date] = None
>
>     contact_email: str
>     max_applicants:Optional[int] = Field(None, ge=1, le=10000)
>
>     @field_validator("required_skills", mode="before")
>     @classmethod
>     def parse_skills(cls, v) -> List[str]:
>         if isinstance(v, str):
>             skills = [s.strip() for s in v.split(",") if s.strip()]
>         elif isinstance(v, list):
>             skills = [str(s).strip() for s in v if s]
>         else:
>             raise ValueError("Skills must be list or comma-separated string")
>         if len(skills) < 1:
>             raise ValueError("At least 1 required skill")
>         if len(skills) > 30:
>             raise ValueError("Maximum 30 skills")
>         return skills
>
>     @field_validator("contact_email")
>     @classmethod
>     def validate_email(cls, v: str) -> str:
>         import re
>         v = v.strip().lower()
>         if not re.match(r'^[^@]+@[^@]+\.[^@]+$', v):
>             raise ValueError(f"Invalid email: {v}")
>         return v
>
>     @model_validator(mode="after")
>     def validate_business_rules(self) -> "JobPosting":
>         errors = []
>
>         # Salary range logic
>         if self.salary_min and self.salary_max:
>             if self.salary_max < self.salary_min:
>                 errors.append("salary_max must be >= salary_min")
>             if self.salary_max > self.salary_min * 10:
>                 errors.append("salary range too wide (max > 10x min)")
>
>         # Experience range logic
>         if (self.experience_max_years is not None and
>                 self.experience_max_years < self.experience_min_years):
>             errors.append("experience_max_years must be >= experience_min_years")
>
>         # Deadline must be in future
>         if (self.application_deadline and
>                 self.application_deadline < date.today()):
>             errors.append("application_deadline must be in the future")
>
>         # Start after deadline
>         if (self.start_date and self.application_deadline and
>                 self.start_date < self.application_deadline):
>             errors.append("start_date must be after application_deadline")
>
>         # Internship salary check
>         if (self.employment_type == "internship" and
>                 self.salary_min and self.salary_min > Decimal("25")):
>             pass  # OK for paid internships
>
>         # Remote job doesn't need specific location
>         if self.remote_policy == "remote" and self.location == "Remote":
>             self.location = "Remote (Worldwide)"
>
>         if errors:
>             raise ValueError(f"Job posting invalid: {'; '.join(errors)}")
>
>         return self
>
> from datetime import timedelta
> today = date.today()
>
> job = JobPosting(
>     title="Senior Python Developer",
>     company_name="Tech Corp",
>     description="We are looking for an experienced Python developer " * 5,
>     required_skills="Python, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, Docker, AWS",
>     employment_type="full_time",
>     location="San Francisco, CA",
>     remote_policy="hybrid",
>     salary_min="120000",
>     salary_max="160000",
>     experience_min_years=3,
>     experience_max_years=8,
>     application_deadline=today + timedelta(days=30),
>     start_date=today + timedelta(days=60),
>     contact_email="HR@TechCorp.COM"
> )
>
> print(f"✅ Job: {job.title}")
> print(f"   Skills : {job.required_skills}")
> print(f"   Salary : ${job.salary_min:,.0f} - ${job.salary_max:,.0f}")
> print(f"   Contact: {job.contact_email}")  # normalized
> ```

sections.title: Pydantic Advanced Features — Conceptual Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
**Q1. What are Generic models in Pydantic and why are they useful?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Generic models use Python's `Generic[T]` to create reusable model templates parameterized by type. Define once, use with any data type. Most common use: API response wrapper — instead of `UserResponse`, `ProductResponse`, `OrderResponse` all with same structure, use one `APIResponse[UserModel]`, `APIResponse[ProductModel]`. Benefits: (1) DRY — response envelope logic written once. (2) Type-safe — IDE knows `response.data` is `UserModel` when you use `APIResponse[UserModel]`. (3) Consistent — all API responses have same structure. (4) Pydantic validates both the wrapper AND the inner type. In FastAPI: `def get_user() -> APIResponse[UserModel]:` gives full OpenAPI schema generation for both layers.

**Q2. What are discriminated unions and when do you use them?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Discriminated unions use a literal "discriminator" field to tell Pydantic which model to use when the input could be one of several types. Without discriminator: Pydantic tries each type in order (slow, may give wrong errors). With discriminator: Pydantic looks at the discriminator field value and picks the exact right model immediately (O(1), better errors). Use when: (1) Webhook payloads — different event types in same field. (2) Notification systems — email/SMS/push in same "notification" field. (3) Shape hierarchy — circle/rectangle/triangle from same "draw" command. (4) Payment methods — credit_card/bank_transfer/crypto in same field. Pattern: each model has `type: Literal["value"]` field, union uses `Field(discriminator="type")`. In production event-driven systems, this is my go-to pattern for heterogeneous event streams.

**Q3. What is `model_copy()` and how does it differ from `model_validate()`?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `model_copy(update={...})` creates a shallow copy of the model with specified fields changed. Validators run on the updated fields. Original model unchanged. `model_validate(data)` creates a brand new model from external data (dict, ORM object, etc.) — full validation from scratch. When to use each: `model_copy` — when you have a valid model and need a slightly modified version (state transitions, applying patches, creating test fixtures). `model_validate` — when reading from external sources (database, API, user input). `model_copy` is much faster than `model_validate` for the unchanged fields. Important: `model_copy(deep=True)` for deep copy of nested models — otherwise nested objects are shared references.

**Q4. How does `model_dump(mode="json")` differ from `model_dump()`?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `model_dump()` returns Python objects — `datetime` stays as `datetime`, `Decimal` stays as `Decimal`, `Enum` stays as Enum member. `model_dump(mode="json")` converts everything to JSON-serializable types — `datetime` → ISO string, `Decimal` → float, `Enum` → value, `bytes` → base64 string, `UUID` → string. Use `mode="json"` when: preparing data for `json.dumps()`, sending to Redis, writing to a file as JSON. Use regular `model_dump()` when: passing to another Python function, SQLAlchemy, further processing in Python. `model_dump_json()` gives the JSON string directly — fastest option for JSON output because it uses Pydantic's Rust-based serializer internally.

**Q5. How do you handle circular references in nested Pydantic models?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Circular references (A → B → A) require forward references:
>
> ```python
> from __future__ import annotations
> from pydantic import BaseModel
> from typing import Optional, List
>
> class Category(BaseModel):
>     name:     str
>     parent:   Optional[Category] = None    # self-reference!
>     children: List[Category] = []         # self-reference!
>
> # model_rebuild() required for self-referential models in v2
> Category.model_rebuild()
>
> root = Category(name="Electronics")
> laptops = Category(name="Laptops", parent=root)
> gaming  = Category(name="Gaming Laptops", parent=laptops)
> ```
>
> For true circular (A→B→A, not just self), use `from __future__ import annotations` at top of file. Pydantic v2 handles this better than v1. In practice, circular model dependencies usually indicate a design issue — consider using IDs instead of nested objects for back-references, and only nest the "child" direction.

**S1. You're building a webhook receiver for multiple services. Design the discriminated union system.**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, field_validator
> from typing import Union, Literal, Annotated, Optional, Dict, Any
> from datetime import datetime
>
> # ── GitHub Webhook Events ─────────────────────────────────────────────
> class GitHubPushEvent(BaseModel):
>     source:       Literal["github"] = "github"
>     event_type:   Literal["push"]   = "push"
>     repository:   str
>     pusher:       str
>     commits:      int
>     branch:       str
>     timestamp:    datetime = Field(default_factory=datetime.now)
>
> class GitHubPREvent(BaseModel):
>     source:       Literal["github"]       = "github"
>     event_type:   Literal["pull_request"] = "pull_request"
>     repository:   str
>     pr_number:    int
>     action:       str  # opened, closed, merged
>     author:       str
>     timestamp:    datetime = Field(default_factory=datetime.now)
>
> # ── Stripe Webhook Events ─────────────────────────────────────────────
> class StripePaymentSucceeded(BaseModel):
>     source:       Literal["stripe"]                = "stripe"
>     event_type:   Literal["payment_intent.succeeded"] = "payment_intent.succeeded"
>     payment_id:   str
>     amount:       int  # in cents
>     currency:     str
>     customer_id:  Optional[str] = None
>     timestamp:    datetime = Field(default_factory=datetime.now)
>
>     @property
>     def amount_dollars(self) -> float:
>         return self.amount / 100
>
> class StripePaymentFailed(BaseModel):
>     source:       Literal["stripe"]             = "stripe"
>     event_type:   Literal["payment_intent.payment_failed"] = "payment_intent.payment_failed"
>     payment_id:   str
>     amount:       int
>     failure_code: str
>     failure_msg:  str
>     timestamp:    datetime = Field(default_factory=datetime.now)
>
> # ── Slack Webhook Events ──────────────────────────────────────────────
> class SlackMessageEvent(BaseModel):
>     source:       Literal["slack"]   = "slack"
>     event_type:   Literal["message"] = "message"
>     channel:      str
>     user:         str
>     text:         str
>     ts:           str  # Slack timestamp
>     timestamp:    datetime = Field(default_factory=datetime.now)
>
> # ── Discriminated Union ───────────────────────────────────────────────
> WebhookEvent = Annotated[
>     Union[
>         GitHubPushEvent, GitHubPREvent,
>         StripePaymentSucceeded, StripePaymentFailed,
>         SlackMessageEvent,
>     ],
>     Field(discriminator="event_type")
> ]
>
> class WebhookEnvelope(BaseModel):
>     webhook_id:  str
>     source:      str
>     signature:   str = ""  # HMAC signature for verification
>     event:       WebhookEvent
>     received_at: datetime = Field(default_factory=datetime.now)
>
>     @field_validator("signature")
>     @classmethod
>     def validate_signature(cls, v: str) -> str:
>         # In production: verify HMAC-SHA256 against secret key
>         return v
>
> # ── Event Router ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
> class WebhookRouter:
>     def __init__(self):
>         self.handlers = {}
>
>     def register(self, event_type: str):
>         def decorator(func):
>             self.handlers[event_type] = func
>             return func
>         return decorator
>
>     def dispatch(self, envelope: WebhookEnvelope):
>         event_type = envelope.event.event_type
>         handler    = self.handlers.get(event_type)
>         if handler:
>             return handler(envelope.event)
>         print(f"  ⚠️  No handler for: {event_type}")
>
> router = WebhookRouter()
>
> @router.register("push")
> def handle_push(event: GitHubPushEvent):
>     print(f"  🔨 GitHub Push: {event.pusher} pushed {event.commits} commits to {event.branch}")
>
> @router.register("payment_intent.succeeded")
> def handle_payment(event: StripePaymentSucceeded):
>     print(f"  💰 Payment succeeded: ${event.amount_dollars:.2f} {event.currency.upper()}")
>
> @router.register("message")
> def handle_slack(event: SlackMessageEvent):
>     print(f"  💬 Slack: {event.user} in #{event.channel}: {event.text[:30]}")
>
> # Test with raw webhook payloads
> raw_webhooks = [
>     {
>         "webhook_id": "WH001", "source": "github",
>         "event": {"event_type": "push", "repository": "myorg/myrepo",
>                   "pusher": "alice", "commits": 3, "branch": "main"}
>     },
>     {
>         "webhook_id": "WH002", "source": "stripe",
>         "event": {"event_type": "payment_intent.succeeded",
>                   "payment_id": "pi_123", "amount": 9999, "currency": "usd"}
>     },
>     {
>         "webhook_id": "WH003", "source": "slack",
>         "event": {"event_type": "message", "channel": "general",
>                   "user": "U001", "text": "Hello team!", "ts": "1234567890.123"}
>     },
> ]
>
> print("Processing webhooks:")
> for raw in raw_webhooks:
>     envelope = WebhookEnvelope.model_validate(raw)
>     router.dispatch(envelope)
> ```

sections.title: Pydantic with Real World — Conceptual Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
**Q1. How do you use Pydantic for settings management in a production application?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Use `pydantic-settings` (`BaseSettings`) which auto-reads from environment variables. Structure: nested models per concern (DatabaseSettings, CacheSettings, APISettings), compose into AppSettings. Benefits: (1) Type validation of env vars (PORT=abc fails immediately). (2) Default values for local dev. (3) `repr=False` on secrets — never appear in logs. (4) `.env` file support out of the box. Pattern:
>
> ```python
> from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
>
> class Settings(BaseSettings):
>     model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
>         env_file=".env", env_nested_delimiter="__"
>     )
>     db_host: str = "localhost"
>     db_port: int = 5432
>     secret_key: str = Field(..., repr=False)
>
> # DB__HOST=prod.db.example.com → settings.db_host = "prod.db.example.com"
> settings = Settings()
> ```
>
> I create a singleton `settings` object imported by all modules. Never pass individual env vars around — always use the settings object for testability.

**Q2. How does Pydantic integrate with FastAPI and what makes it powerful?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> FastAPI is built ON TOP of Pydantic — every parameter, body, response, and query string is a Pydantic model. Integration: (1) **Auto-validation** — FastAPI calls `model_validate()` on request bodies automatically, returns 422 with Pydantic errors if invalid. (2) **OpenAPI/Swagger** — FastAPI reads `model_json_schema()` to generate API documentation automatically. (3) **Response serialization** — `response_model=UserResponse` tells FastAPI to call `model_dump()` and validate the response. (4) **Dependency injection** — Pydantic models as query params with `Query()`. (5) **Type conversion** — path params, query strings auto-converted to declared types. In a 100k+ line production codebase, this means almost zero manual validation code — Pydantic/FastAPI handles it all.

**Q3. How do you design the Pydantic model layer for a database-backed API?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> I use 4 model types per entity: (1) **Base** — shared fields (username, email). (2) **Create** — for POST requests, includes password, excludes auto-fields. (3) **Update** — for PATCH, all fields Optional. (4) **Response** — for GET, excludes password, includes computed fields, `from_attributes=True`. Additionally: **DB model** (SQLAlchemy) stays separate from Pydantic. `from_attributes=True` bridges them. Never use same model for input and output — security risk. Example:
>
> ```
> UserBase → UserCreate (POST body)
>         → UserUpdate (PATCH body)
>         → UserResponse (GET response)
>         → UserWithPosts (GET /users/{id}/with-posts)
> ```
>
> Repository layer converts ORM → Pydantic: `return UserResponse.model_validate(db_user)`. This is clean separation of concerns.

**Q4. How do you handle validation errors in a production API?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Never expose raw Pydantic `ValidationError` to clients — transform it:
>
> ```python
> from fastapi import Request
> from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse
> from pydantic import ValidationError
>
> # Global exception handler in FastAPI
> @app.exception_handler(ValidationError)
> async def validation_handler(req: Request, exc: ValidationError):
>     errors = [
>         {
>             "field":   ".".join(str(l) for l in e["loc"]),
>             "message": e["msg"],
>             "code":    e["type"],
>         }
>         for e in exc.errors()
>     ]
>     return JSONResponse(
>         status_code=422,
>         content={
>             "success": False,
>             "errors":  errors,
>             "message": "Validation failed"
>         }
>     )
> ```
>
> Log the full error internally, return clean user-facing messages. Map Pydantic error types to user-friendly messages: `string_too_short` → "Must be at least N characters". `value_error` → your custom message. `missing` → "This field is required".

**Q5. How do you test Pydantic models effectively?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Test all validation paths: happy path, each constraint violation, edge cases:
>
> ```python
> import pytest
> from pydantic import ValidationError
>
> class TestUserModel:
>     def test_valid_user(self):
>         user = User(username="alice", email="alice@ex.com", age=30)
>         assert user.username == "alice"
>         assert user.email == "alice@ex.com"
>
>     def test_email_normalized(self):
>         user = User(username="bob", email="BOB@EXAMPLE.COM", age=25)
>         assert user.email == "bob@example.com"  # lowercased
>
>     def test_invalid_email(self):
>         with pytest.raises(ValidationError) as exc:
>             User(username="carol", email="not-valid", age=30)
>         errors = exc.value.errors()
>         assert any(e["loc"] == ("email",) for e in errors)
>
>     def test_age_constraints(self):
>         with pytest.raises(ValidationError):
>             User(username="dave", email="d@ex.com", age=-1)
>         with pytest.raises(ValidationError):
>             User(username="dave", email="d@ex.com", age=200)
>
>     def test_type_coercion(self):
>         user = User(username="eve", email="e@ex.com", age="28")  # string age
>         assert user.age == 28
>         assert isinstance(user.age, int)
> ```
>
> Also test: `model_dump()` output, `model_validate()` from dict/JSON, cross-field validators, `model_copy()` behavior.

**S1. You're migrating a Flask app to FastAPI. How do you design the Pydantic model layer?**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, field_validator
> from typing import Optional, List
> from datetime import datetime
> from decimal import Decimal
>
> # ── Step 1: Define base model with common config ──────────────────────
> class BaseSchema(BaseModel):
>     model_config = ConfigDict(
>         from_attributes=True,   # SQLAlchemy compatibility
>         populate_by_name=True,
>         str_strip_whitespace=True,
>         use_enum_values=True,
>     )
>
> # ── Step 2: One entity = multiple schemas ─────────────────────────────
> # Products
> class ProductBase(BaseSchema):
>     name:        str = Field(..., min_length=2, max_length=200)
>     description: str = Field("", max_length=2000)
>     price:       Decimal = Field(..., gt=0, decimal_places=2)
>     category:    str
>
> class ProductCreate(ProductBase):
>     """POST /products — what client sends"""
>     sku:         str = Field(..., pattern=r'^[A-Z]{2}-\d{4}$')
>     cost_price:  Decimal = Field(..., gt=0, decimal_places=2, exclude=True)
>
> class ProductUpdate(BaseSchema):
>     """PATCH /products/{id} — partial update"""
>     name:        Optional[str] = Field(None, min_length=2, max_length=200)
>     description: Optional[str] = None
>     price:       Optional[Decimal] = Field(None, gt=0, decimal_places=2)
>     category:    Optional[str] = None
>     is_active:   Optional[bool] = None
>
> class ProductResponse(ProductBase):
>     """GET /products — what API returns"""
>     product_id:  int
>     sku:         str
>     is_active:   bool
>     created_at:  datetime
>     # cost_price NOT included — sensitive business data!
>
> class ProductListResponse(ProductResponse):
>     """In list view — minimal fields"""
>     pass  # same for now, could remove description
>
> # ── Step 3: Use in FastAPI endpoints ─────────────────────────────────
> # (Pseudocode — shows the pattern)
> #
> # @app.post("/products", response_model=ProductResponse, status_code=201)
> # async def create_product(data: ProductCreate, db: Session = Depends(get_db)):
> #     db_product = ProductORM(**data.model_dump(exclude_unset=True))
> #     db.add(db_product)
> #     db.commit()
> #     return ProductResponse.model_validate(db_product)
> #
> # @app.patch("/products/{id}", response_model=ProductResponse)
> # async def update_product(id: int, data: ProductUpdate,
> #                          db: Session = Depends(get_db)):
> #     product = db.get(ProductORM, id)
> #     # Only update provided fields (exclude_unset!)
> #     update_data = data.model_dump(exclude_unset=True)
> #     for field, value in update_data.items():
> #         setattr(product, field, value)
> #     db.commit()
> #     return ProductResponse.model_validate(product)
>
> # Test the schema layer
> product_data = {
>     "name": "  Python Handbook  ",
>     "description": "Complete Python reference",
>     "price": "49.99",
>     "category": "books",
>     "sku": "BK-0001",
>     "cost_price": "15.00",
> }
>
> create_req = ProductCreate.model_validate(product_data)
> print(f"Create request:")
> print(f"  Name    : '{create_req.name}'")  # stripped!
> print(f"  Price   : {create_req.price}")
>
> # cost_price excluded from dump (sensitive)
> dump = create_req.model_dump()
> print(f"  Has cost_price: {'cost_price' in dump}")  # False!
>
> # Simulate DB object
> class FakeProductDB:
>     product_id=1; name="Python Handbook"; description="Complete Python reference"
>     price=Decimal("49.99"); category="books"; sku="BK-0001"
>     is_active=True; created_at=datetime.now()
>
> response = ProductResponse.model_validate(FakeProductDB())
> print(f"\nResponse: {response.name} — ${response.price}")
> ```

quiz.question: What is a dataclass and what boilerplate code does it automatically generate?
options: 5-Year Exp Answer: > Pydantic handles nested models automatically.
5-Year Exp Answer: > Regular Enum members use identity comparison — two members are equal only if they're the same member.
5-Year Exp Answer: > order=True generates __lt__, __le__, __gt__, __ge__ — making instances sortable and comparable with , =.
5-Year Exp Answer: > A dataclass is a Python decorator (@dataclass) introduced in Python 3.7 (PEP 557) that automatically generates boilerplate special methods for…
quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: A dataclass is a Python decorator (@dataclass) introduced in Python 3.7 (PEP 557) that automatically generates boilerplate special methods for classes whose primary purpose is storing data. By default it generates: __init__() (constructor with all fields as parameters), __repr__() (human-readable string representation), and __eq__() (equality comparison that compares all fields).

quiz.question: What is the difference between a dataclass and a regular Python class?
options: 5-Year Exp Answer: > extra="forbid" raises ValidationError if the input contains any fields not defined in the model.
5-Year Exp Answer: > Circular references (A → B → A) require forward references: > > > > For true circular (A→B→A, not just self), use from __future__ import annotations…
